prize_parts.citation: for establishing nominal rigidities, staggered price and wage setting and interest-rate rules as the micro-founded basis of modern monetary policy analysis

statement.case_for: The New Keynesian framework is the one macroeconomic paradigm in this pool that has changed both academic modelling and day-to-day policy practice for decades. The three proposed names map onto three distinct conceptual steps. Calvo supplied the tractable time-dependent pricing device that makes a forward-looking Phillips curve possible. Taylor supplied staggered contracting and the policy-rule idea that disciplined thinking about systematic policy. Woodford supplied the integrated microfounded synthesis, including welfare-based optimal policy. The work is mature, with 25 to 40 years of testing. It has been stress-tested through the zero lower bound, the 2008 crisis and the post-2020 inflation, and in each case it was extended rather than discarded. It also supplies the baseline that heterogeneous-agent extensions (my own field) build on or criticise, which is itself evidence of foundational status. Monetary-policy macro has been recognised before (rational expectations, time consistency, VAR methods, banking and crises), but the nominal-rigidity and policy-rule core has not.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the main weakness. Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Gertler and Smets and Wouters made major theoretical and empirical contributions, and a three-name cap leaves several of them out. The framework's forecasting and policy performance around 2008 and 2021-22 is contested. Representative-agent versions are widely seen as superseded by heterogeneous-agent models, so a prize risks rewarding a stage in the field's development rather than its end state.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B014 second and proposes Woodford, Gali and Taylor. He argues credit is highly diffuse, that Gali covers the empirical and analytical framework, and that monetary macro may be relatively saturated given earlier prizes to Lucas, Kydland and Prescott, Sargent and Sims, and Bernanke.
responses.response: I take the attribution point seriously and agree that any trio is contestable. Gali's New Keynesian Phillips curve and policy analysis is a genuine claim. I still prefer Calvo over Gali. Calvo's pricing device is the primitive on which both the Gali and the Woodford derivations rest, and it is a more distinct conceptual step than the later development and estimation work. I would regard Gali as the strongest omitted claimant, not as a weaker one. On saturation, I do not think earlier prizes cover this core. They went to rational expectations, time consistency, identification and banking crises, not to nominal rigidities and policy rules as such. Saturation is therefore a smaller concern than attribution.

responses.point: Stromberg ranks B003 first and proposes Moore, Kiyotaki and Gertler. He argues the collateral-constraint and financial-accelerator mechanism is foundational for macro-finance and for understanding the 2008 crisis, and that the 2022 prize makes this related rather than duplicative.
responses.response: I agree B003 is a strong candidate and I ranked it third. Kiyotaki and Moore have the cleanest two-person attribution in the pool, and the mechanism has aged well. I differ on two points. First, the 2022 prize covered much of the same crisis territory, and I think the marginal distinctiveness is narrower than for the nominal-rigidity core. Second, adding Gertler muddies the attribution, because his contributions run through both B003 and B014 and the financial-accelerator side is tied to an existing laureate. I would keep B003 as a two-person case. If the committee judges the crisis-mechanism question more pressing than monetary policy, it is a defensible alternative.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B030 (Grossman and Helpman) first because the credit sits in a clean, long-standing two-person partnership, and he ranks B014 second, noting that attribution is the main difficulty there.
responses.response: Hassler is right that B030 has the cleaner attribution, and I accept that on the narrow ground of credit. Attribution is not the only criterion, though. I would weigh how much the work changed the practice of the field, and here I think B014 is stronger. Protection for Sale has mixed empirical support, as Hassler himself notes, and the committee would have to explain how it differs from the 2008 trade prize. If the committee wants a trade prize, I find Melitz and Helpman (B047) the more convincing case. I do not rank B030 above B014 simply because its credit is easier to assign.

uncertainties: Whether Gali, or Christiano and Eichenbaum, should replace Calvo or Taylor, and whether the committee would accept the omission of the estimated-DSGE strand.
How much weight to give post-2021 inflation performance and the heterogeneous-agent critique against a prize for the representative-agent framework.
Whether the 2022 prize leaves enough room for B003, and whether Gertler belongs there or in B014.
Whether a narrower citation (pricing friction only, or policy rule only) would make attribution cleaner than the broad framework citation.
statement.conflict_note: None specific to the B014 names is apparent from the supplied profile, which lists no co-authorship with Calvo, Taylor or Woodford. Proximity is of field only: I work in macroeconomic theory, including heterogeneous-agent models that extend or criticise this framework. My listed long-term co-authors include committee members Hassler and Boppart, who are not candidates. Of the other shortlisted entries, I note that Boppart co-authored with Klenow (B013), though that is Boppart's own disclosure and not mine. B032 is an alternative only. The profile does not state Persson's affiliation, but my institution, the IIES in Stockholm, is closely associated with political economics, so a possible institutional connection there should be noted. Conflicts are disclosed, not adjudicated.
